analysis.one_liner: Sets a schedule for airliners to install a midair collision avoidance system.
analysis.headline: The bill passed the House by voice vote in July 1989, but the Senate never voted on it and let it die by postponing it indefinitely in October 1990.
analysis.plain_summary: After a series of deadly midair collisions, this bill would have required airliners with more than 30 seats to carry TCAS-II, an onboard system that warns pilots when another aircraft is on a collision course. Before the bill reached the House floor, the committee stripped out the actual installation requirement, leaving only a mandate for the FAA to run a one-year evaluation of the system and permission for the FAA to push back installation deadlines. The House passed that weaker version by voice vote, but the Senate committee forwarded it without a recommendation and the Senate never took it up.
analysis.who_benefits: Airline passengers and crews, who get a second line of defense against midair collisions; also the avionics companies that would build and install the systems.

how_it_helps.text: The original bill required civil aircraft with more than 30 passenger seats to be equipped with the TCAS-II collision avoidance system on a set installation schedule.
The FAA would have had to run a one-year operational evaluation of TCAS-II to collect safety and operational data from equipped aircraft, including from foreign carriers.

The bill directed the FAA to consider coordinating the wind shear equipment installation schedule with the collision avoidance system schedule, so aircraft would not face conflicting retrofit timelines.

analysis.who_pays: Airlines, which would bear the cost of buying and installing TCAS-II units in their fleets, a cost likely passed into fares.
analysis.who_pays_short: Commercial airlines and their passengers' fares

drawbacks.text: Equipping an entire large-aircraft fleet with TCAS-II is expensive, and the original mandate would have imposed that cost on airlines on a fixed statutory schedule, which is why flexibility for a 'safe and orderly transition' was written in.

The version that actually passed the House contained no installation requirement at all — the committee deleted the mandate, leaving only an FAA evaluation study, so the bill as passed would not by itself have put a single new unit on an aircraft.

The bill as passed also let the FAA extend the existing installation deadline by up to two years, and further with written notice to Congress, which could delay the safety benefit it was meant to speed up.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety benefit is real — onboard collision avoidance directly prevents midair crashes of the kind that killed everyone aboard two aircraft over Cerritos, California in 1986. But the bill that reached the Senate had already been hollowed out: the installation mandate was stripped in committee, leaving a study and deadline flexibility. The cost to airlines was the legitimate objection, and Congress chose to handle it through amendment and delay rather than the original hard schedule.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it by voice vote, but the Senate committee sent it to the floor with no recommendation, the Senate never voted, and in October 1990 it was indefinitely postponed — set aside with no objection — until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ron Packard introduced the bill on April 27, 1989 to require TCAS-II collision avoidance equipment in aircraft with more than 30 seats, with no cosponsors.

The House Public Works and Transportation Committee amended the bill before reporting it, and the amended version dropped the installation mandate, keeping only the operational evaluation program and the wind shear compatibility provision.
The House passed the amended bill by voice vote on July 31, 1989 under a procedure that allows passage with limited debate and no recorded roll call.
The Senate Commerce Committee reported the bill in November 1989 without a recommendation, adding an extension of an FAA civil penalty demonstration program, and placed it on the Senate calendar.

The bill sat on the Senate calendar for nearly a year; on October 5, 1990 the Senate indefinitely postponed it by unanimous consent, and the House action record points instead to separate bills, H.R. 3402 and H.R. 3671.
The 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 without the Senate ever voting on the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Airlines came out ahead: the hard installation mandate was stripped before the House vote, and the remaining shell died without a Senate vote, so no new statutory deadlines ever took effect. Airline passengers did not get the bill's added safety requirement through this legislation.

sides.party_line_note: The House passed it by voice vote with no recorded roll call, a Republican introduced it, and a Senate run by Democrats let it die, so no party split is visible in the record.

industries.note: The original bill would have forced airlines to buy and install TCAS-II on a fixed schedule; the amended version dropped that mandate and instead let the FAA push installation deadlines back by up to two years. Either way, the airlines' interest in this bill ran against the passenger safety mandate.
A TCAS-II mandate would have created a guaranteed market for the companies building the collision avoidance units and their installation. Their interest in the bill ran alongside passenger safety.
The bill directed the FAA to consider aligning the wind shear equipment retrofit schedule with the TCAS-II schedule, which would affect the timing of that equipment market without changing its size.
